# ChipStain — video script (generated by scripts/build_slides.py — edit writeup/slides_template.json, not this file)

The narrated draft video `writeup/video/ChipStain_video.mp4` is built from these slides and lines by `scripts/build_video.py`. For the submission you may instead record yourself over the same slides; replace slides 4–5 with a live screen recording of `python demo/app.py` (examples `example_bf_dense_t150.tif` and `example_bf_dense_t150_blur1px.tif`, TTA on) to show the real system running.

| # | Slide | Narration |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | ChipStain | We are team Hack2Publish — Hamid, Esfer and Foysal — and this is ChipStain, in the Model and Algorithm category. |
| 2 | Nuclear read-outs need a stain — and a stain has a cost | Almost every read-out on an organ-on-a-chip — cell number, growth, viability — starts from a nuclear stain. But fixation ends the experiment, live DNA dyes are phototoxic, and reporter lines are rarely available for iPSC-derived tissue such as neurons. In-silico labeling can predict the stain from a bright-field image, but a plain prediction gives no warning when it is wrong. |
| 3 | Predict the stain and its uncertainty | ChipStain is a U-Net whose head predicts, for every pixel, a mean and a variance, trained with the beta N L L loss. At test time we average eight flipped and rotated views; their disagreement is added to the learned variance. Nothing here is a new mechanism. What we contribute is testing whether this uncertainty actually helps, against honest baselines. |
| 4 | 183 nuclei found — the reference has 180 | Here is a bright-field image from a well the model never saw. On a laptop CPU we get the predicted nuclear stain and the uncertainty map. Sigma is higher on nuclei — brighter means noisier — and near zero on background. The app counts 183 nuclei; the dataset's reference annotation has 180. |
| 5 | The prediction fails — and σ says so | Now the same image, slightly blurred — a crude stand-in for defocus. The prediction falls apart, and the uncertainty jumps from 0.08 to 0.33; the app warns that the input looks unlike its training data. A plain U-Net in this situation becomes less uncertain — it fails silently. |
| 6 | Same fidelity, much better uncertainty | Over three training runs on 125 test images, ChipStain matches a U-Net with the same augmentation in correlation with the real stain — 0.768 versus 0.764 — at a 10 percent higher pixel error. Its uncertainty ranks errors clearly better — Spearman 0.47 versus 0.28, in every test field and every seed — and it is close to calibrated: the 95 percent interval covers 92 percent of pixels. |
| 7 | When the input drifts, σ rises — the baseline's falls | We stressed both models with blur, noise and a different imaging modality. Both predictions break, ChipStain's more. But its uncertainty rises several-fold and flags the failed images, while the baseline's uncertainty falls — it fails silently. |
| 8 | 60 hours of growth from bright-field alone | On a 60-hour time-lapse, counting nuclei on the prediction gives a doubling time of 24.9 hours, against 23.9 from the real stain. And an uncertainty gate fixed on validation data cuts the doubling-time error across training runs from 9.1 to 4.1 percent. |
| 9 | What σ does not do | To be clear about the limits: if you only need a nuclear count, a segmentation model trained on matching labels does better — Cellpose reaches F1 0.831 versus our 0.708. Per-nucleus sigma is no better than a simple brightness rule. And we had no organ-on-chip images. On human stem-cell-derived motor neurons, the model transfers partly even without retraining, and fine-tuning on a single well raises the correlation from 0.59 to 0.76.  |
| 10 | github.com/hamidhosen42/AI4S-Open-Innovation-AI-for-Life-Science | Everything is open: code, weights, data links, a CPU inference script — and one script regenerates every number, figure, this deck and the report. Thank you. |

Narration: 483 words.
